title: The Throne That Was Never Meant to Be
subtitle: Krishna crowns Ugrasena king of the Yadavas
story:
Mathura had a king all along — he had simply been in prison for years.

Ugrasena, Kamsa's father, had been pushed aside and locked away by his own son, who had taken the throne and ruled the city through fear. In all the years of Kamsa's reign, through the killings, the taxes, the arena, few had dared to remember the old man in the cell. But when Krishna had freed his parents and the dust of the arena had settled, he did not sit on the empty throne himself. He went to the prison, released his grandfather from confinement, and led him out into the light of the city his son had stolen from him.

Then, before the assembled Yadavas, Krishna declared that Ugrasena would be king. And he explained why the throne had to pass to him, and not to the young conqueror whom every hand in the city would have raised up. Long ago, he said, a curse had been laid upon the Yadava line: because of Yayati's curse, no Yadava was to sit on the throne. The kingship of the Yadavas was a charge to be held, not a prize to be taken, and it could not be held by one who was born under that curse. So the man who had actually won the city would serve, and the man the curse allowed would rule.

Ugrasena did not want it. He had seen what the throne had done to his son; he had spent years in a cell because of it. He spoke of performing the rites and retiring to the forest with his wife and daughters-in-law, and pressed Kamsa's kingdom and wealth upon Krishna; but Krishna refused, saying he cared nothing for the kingdom or the royal throne, and instructed his grandfather to place himself on the throne and win glory by becoming king. But Krishna, who knew the law, would not be moved. The Harivamsha remembers his reply in the form of an instruction: place yourself on the throne, and acquire victory by becoming the king. And so Govinda, well read in the laws, installed his grandfather on the throne that his son's death had left vacant.

There was a strangeness in the coronation that the city felt without quite understanding. The boy from Gokula, who had arrived in Mathura that morning as a stranger and left it the master of everything, stood at the foot of the throne and placed an old man upon it — an old man who had been robbed of that very seat by the tyrant Krishna had just slain. He did not take the crown, the wealth, or the army; he gave them all to the man Kamsa had wronged. The Yadava chiefs and the citizens looked at the old king, and at the young man who refused to be king, and understood that they had been given something stranger than a victory — they had been given justice.

Ugrasena took his seat, and Mathura had a king again, and the king was the man Kamsa had tried to erase. Krishna had said that while he served at his grandfather's side, the very gods themselves would pay tribute to the throne. The city could not see the gods, but it could see this: the tyrant's line was over, the old king had come home, and the boy who had done it all asked for nothing — not the throne, not the crown, not a single measure of the wealth lying in Kamsa's halls.

The yoke of the Yadava kingship had been carried by a usurper for years. Now it rested on the shoulders it had always belonged to, and the man who had won it back stood below it, content to serve.
reflection: Krishna wins Mathura and immediately gives it away — to the grandfather Kamsa had imprisoned. His power is expressed as service: he refuses the throne not out of modesty but out of law, honoring the old curse on the Yadava line by letting the lawful king rule while he himself stands below the throne.
tradition_note: The Vishnu Purana tells the same crowning in its chapter on Kamsa's funeral rites, folding the consolation of the widows into the same episode; the Bhagavata keeps the coronation and the mourning separate, and this story follows it. The Yayati curse is given only in summary in the sources.
next_story_tease: With a king at last upon the throne, there remained the wounded city and the Yadavas to be gathered.
hero_scene: Krishna placing his grandfather Ugrasena upon the throne of Mathura in the great hall, the assembled Yadavas and citizens watching, the old king seated while Krishna stands below him with folded hands.
